milestones.name: A second engine module reads cooked volumes and textures in its own passes and follows edits to them, on Mac and in Chrome
milestones.bar: Residency that behaves like streaming in a shipped open-world game such as Marvel's Spider-Man 2: content arrives over several frames and none of them is late, a product is never seen half-loaded, and a failed load leaves the last good one in use.

items.statement: A contribution that holds only a lease binds twelve cooked 128-cubed volumes and one 2D texture in its own pass. On the portable profile every texel of every mip it fetches equals the mapped product's bytes. On the Mac's preferred profile it is lent the BC4 volumes, and their base level fetched on the GPU meets the 30 dB floor that cooked_texture_quality already holds compressed products to.
items.ask: Read the test. Does the consumer reach the textures only through the public lease, with no access to residency's internals, the store or a loader of its own? Are the portable texels compared with bytes mapped through thrum-asset, for every mip?

items.statement: A lease offers a publication's products only once every copy is in a submitted frame, and always as a whole set. The frame that records the last copy still offers the old set, and so does the next frame when that one is discarded. The first frame recorded after it is submitted offers the new set. A publication superseded while it uploads is never offered.
items.ask: Does the test discard the frame that records the last copy before it asserts what the consumer was offered, and does it supersede a set that is still uploading?

items.statement: An edit to one volume reaches the consumer as a change to that product alone, and stays pending until a submitted frame that advances history has used the new view: a discarded frame or a capture that uses it first does not lose it. The other eleven keep their identity, textures and views, and only the edited product's bytes are uploaded. The consumer makes a new bind group and no pipeline, on both profiles.
items.ask: Does the test discard the first frame that uses the new view, and in another run make that frame a capture, and then assert the diagnostic consumer still applies its invalidation in the next submitted frame that advances history, and in no frame after it?

items.statement: With placements and a lease loading together, the copies recorded in any one frame stay within the one upload budget and staging never holds more than the ring's bound. The upload bench records the first load of the twelve volumes and a one-volume edit, with render-thread time on upload frames beside steady frames.
items.ask: Does the cooked_edit bench carry a leased scenario, recorded with its load class? Do its upload frames' render-thread times sit within the spread of its steady frames, and if not, is the cause named?

items.statement: When a staging chunk cannot be filled, its slot is freed, the error is recorded once, the pending set is dropped, and the drawn and lent sets stay as they were; the next publication uploads within the staging bound. A publication in which a leased product is missing, invalid or refused for the device is refused whole: placements and leases both keep the last good generation, and the record names the product and the reason.
items.ask: Is the fault injected where a chunk is mapped or written, so that the production failure branch is the code that runs? Does an ordinary build compile without the probe?

items.statement: After device replacement the lease is empty until the same content is staged again on the new device. The consumer rebuilds on the new generation, holds no view of the old one and reads the same texels again.

In Chrome, from a fetched store, the consumer reads the same portable texels for the twelve volumes and the texture; an edited volume reaches the consumer as one change with one product fetched; and after a device loss and recovery the set is lent again.

The lease is documented for the modules that will use it: what a consumer names, what it is offered and when, what it must do on a change, including when the frame that first used the new view is discarded or is a capture, and on a new device generation, and what residency never does for it.
items.ask: Could the SEA or CLOUDS planner write a pass that samples a cooked volume or a foam texture from the public documentation and this design alone? Does the lease's public surface name any game type, sea or cloud concept, or placement?

items.statement: Every registered exact baseline, on the Mac and in Chrome, passes the verifier at the claimed commit: this milestone moved no retained image.

A texture that a placement samples and a lease lends changes through both in the same submitted frame. Every submitted frame across the edit shows the old texture on the mesh and in the consumer's pass, or the new one in both; none shows one of each. This holds when the switch frame is discarded, and with the consumer before or after residency in the scene's contribution list.
items.ask: Does the test compare the placement's pixels and the consumer's output in every submitted frame from the first copy to the frame after the switch, each against all-old and all-new references? Does it run with the consumer on each side of residency in the contribution list, and once with the switch frame discarded?

milestones.name: An edited mesh changes on every entity that uses it while the game runs, with no pixel different from a fresh start, on Mac and in Chrome
milestones.bar: Hot reload as in Unreal Engine's static-mesh reimport or Bevy's asset hot reloading, without their hitch: the edited mesh replaces the old one on every entity in one frame, and that frame is exactly the one a fresh launch would draw.

items.statement: A cooked mesh product becomes a mesh row whose positions, UVs and indices equal the product's exactly and whose normals are its decoded normals. A product the arena would refuse (non-finite data, an index out of range, a coordinate past the limit, over capacity) is refused with a named reason and never drawn.

After a cooked mesh that entities draw is edited while the game runs, every later frame equals, byte for byte, a scene prepared fresh from the edited store, in Direct, Frustum and Occlusion with Sun shadows on. The entities' slots, rows and bucket membership are unchanged.
items.ask: Is the fresh scene prepared in a separate host from the edited store, and compared at the same tick and view? Does one edit grow the mesh past its old bounds and another shrink it, each changing the vertex and index counts, so that a stale range or bound would show?

items.statement: While a replacement is written, every frame draws the old mesh whole. Every reader of the row switches in one submitted frame. A discarded switch frame commits nothing, and the next frame records the same switch, also when a newer edit has arrived behind it. A newer edit that supersedes a replacement still being written leaves the old mesh drawn. The old geometry's arena space is reused only after the switch frame is submitted.
items.ask: Does the test compare every submitted frame across the write and the switch with the all-old or the all-new reference, including the frame after a discarded switch frame, the frames after a newer edit arrives behind a discarded switch frame, and the frames after a newer edit supersedes a replacement still being written? Do the arena write, the row switch and the retirement of old space all go through the frame host, so that its exclusive encoded-frame token is what keeps a switch from overtaking an unsubmitted frame, and does the test drive that protocol without reaching around the token?

items.statement: The row bytes written in any one frame stay within the route's bound whatever the mesh's size. An edit that fits the arena's free space uploads only that row. Repeated edits of one mesh reuse retired space, so the arena does not grow with the number of edits. An edit creates no pipeline and compiles no graph. The bound and its measured render-thread time are recorded.

A replacement the arena refuses, or a broken source, leaves the old row drawing and records the reason; the next good edit replaces it. After a resize and after device replacement the scene draws the newest committed rows, equal to a fresh scene from the same store.

In Chrome the valley's entities draw cooked mesh rows from the fetched store. An edited mesh changes on every entity that uses it with one product fetched and no page reload, and the paused canvas after the edit equals a fresh page on the edited store.
In real time on the Mac the edited mesh replaces the old one on every entity in one frame: no entity goes missing, no frame mixes old and new, and its shadow changes with it.
items.inspect: Capture with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode on the valley with cooked mesh rows and a moving camera: one edit that grows a prop mesh and one that shrinks it. Judge the frames around each switch whole and in native-size crops, as consecutive frames at 1x.

items.statement: Every registered exact baseline, on the Mac and in Chrome, passes the verifier at the claimed commit: this milestone moved no retained image.

A cooked mesh that is both placed and an entity's mesh row changes through both in the same submitted frame, however many frames the row's write takes. Every submitted frame across the edit shows the old mesh in both, with its shadows, or the new mesh in both. When the arena refuses the replacement, the placement keeps the old mesh too, and so does every other product of that publication.
items.ask: Is the replacement large enough that the row's write is still going for several frames after residency's last copy was submitted, and does the test compare every submitted frame in that interval, whole, with all-old and all-new references? Does it discard the switch frame once? In the refusal case, does the publication also change a texture, and does the test show that texture unchanged?

milestones.name: Edits to meshes, textures and volumes appear in the running valley without a hitch, on Mac and in Chrome, and the content gate closes
milestones.bar: A content loop a creator trusts, as live reimport is in Unreal Engine or Unity, at the smoothness of a shipped high-end game: saving a file changes the running valley within a moment, no frame is late or half-drawn because of it, nothing ghosts under reconstruction, and a bad save never takes the picture away.

items.statement: In the running valley on the Mac with reconstruction on, three edits each appear: a mesh that is both placed and an entity's mesh row, a texture that a placement samples and a lease lends, and a leased volume. In every submitted frame of an edit window the game's frame record shows one generation through every reader. The frame records, taken with capture off, show edit windows no slower than the steady windows of the same run. The G5 tripwires hold against their load-class history.
items.ask: Do the frame records come from the game's frame host on its ordinary frame path, with the recipe, whether a drawable was presented, and the generation each reader showed? Is any frame in an edit window longer than the longest steady frame of the same run, and if so is its cause named and outside this module?

items.statement: On the Mac each edit appears whole in one frame under reconstruction, through every reader at once: no partly loaded texture or volume, no missing or mixed mesh, no frame with the new mesh where it is placed and the old one on the entities, no flash, and no ghost or smear of the old content in the frames after.
items.inspect: Capture with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode on the valley with TAAU and a moving camera: a mesh that is both placed and an entity's mesh row, a texture that a placement samples and a lease lends, and a leased volume, with both readers of each shared product in view. Judge the eight frames around each switch whole and in native-size crops, as consecutive frames at 1x.

items.statement: In Chrome the same three edits appear on the running page with one switch each and only the changed products fetched, and every submitted frame of an edit window shows one generation through every reader. At the product sizes the valley and the twelve-volume fixture use, no edit makes a frame late: the page's frame-callback intervals in edit windows are recorded beside steady windows of the same run.
items.ask: At the product sizes the valley and the twelve-volume fixture use, is any interval in an edit window longer than the longest steady interval of the same run? If so, is its cause named and outside this module? A stall this module causes at those sizes fails the item and is fixed, not explained. Separately, does the evidence record the larger product size at which a frame is first lost? That figure is a measurement and gates nothing.

items.statement: In Chrome each edit appears whole in one frame under reconstruction, through every reader at once, with no partly loaded product, missing mesh, flash or ghost.
items.inspect: Capture with T2 engine capture in `realtime` mode in Chrome on the valley with TAAU: the same three edits, with both readers of each shared product in view. Judge the frames around each switch whole and in native-size crops, as consecutive frames at 1x.

items.statement: A broken glTF, a glTF saved without its buffer, a truncated texture, a volume the device cannot hold and a save made during a cook each leave the last good content drawing with the reason recorded, and the corrected file publishes normally, from a mapped store and from a fetched one.
items.ask: For each bad save in this list, which test shows the previous content still drawn and the reason recorded, on the mapped store and on the fetched feed? Name any case with no test.

items.statement: No shipping package links the cooker: the dependency graphs of the shipping packages and the symbols of a release shipping binary hold no authoring code, and the same scan finds it in the cooker.

A watcher publication is a preview that changes presentation only: nothing in simulation, collision, navigation or activation reads a cooked product. An incomplete save that still validates may be shown as it stands, and the finished save then publishes exactly what a fresh cook of the finished sources publishes.
items.ask: Which code paths read products published through the watcher or the dev server, and is any of them outside presentation? Does the test publish an intermediate state that validates (a changed glTF over its old buffer) before the buffer is saved, and then compare the final manifest's product hashes with a fresh cook of the finished sources in an empty store? Do the design, the ledger and the G5 decision claim only this, and not that an incomplete save is refused?

items.statement: Gate G5 holds as the brief words it, and the maturity ledger and the G5 decision say what was and was not proved.
items.ask: Take gate G5's clauses in the brief one at a time. Does each have evidence at the claimed commit? Does the ledger keep implementation, correctness, visuals and device results apart, and name what is parked (CAS collection, the iPhone volume encoding, parameter files as a product, source admission and with it a boundary for an external save) and what is unmeasured (a physical iPhone, sustained runs, physical residency)? Does the G5 decision's capability table match the code?

items.statement: The public documentation tells a creator how a saved file reaches the running game, what a bad save does and what an incomplete save can show until it is finished, and tells an engine module how to take placements, cooked mesh rows and leases.
items.ask: Could SHOWCASE's planner give the exit scene's entities cooked meshes, and a creator follow an edit from save to screen, from the public documentation alone?

items.statement: Every registered exact baseline, on the Mac and in Chrome, passes the verifier at the claimed commit: this milestone moved no retained image.
